(CNN) -- The economic downturn may take its toll at the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday night. But as always, the show will go on. Eli Roth and Brad Pitt are men on a mission in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds." Studios are cutting back on parties and all the glitz that goes with them, according to news reports. Moreover, there will be fewer people around to cover Cannes, as news organizations around the world trim costs. (Several, in fact, have tightened up by eliminating their movie reviewers.) Nevertheless, those who attend may see a bumper crop of good and intriguing films, Variety's Jay Weissberg told Reuters. "We've all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have." Leah Rozen, film critic for People magazine, said there are several promising contenders for the Palme d'Or, Cannes' top prize, as well as a number of notable movies premiering out of competition. "What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema," she said. "This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition."  See Rozen talk about some of this year's promising works » . Two of the films in competition are American: Quentin Tarantino's World War II movie, "Inglourious Basterds," and Ang Lee's "Taking Woodstock," a tale about the 1969 music festival. Tarantino told The New York Times that he's been hoping to do a war movie for years. "You've got to make a movie about something, and I'm a film guy, so I think in terms of genres," he said. However, the maker of "Pulp Fiction" and "Jackie Brown" added, that doesn't mean what he ends up with resembles what he started with: "It's simply the spark that starts the fire." "Inglourious Basterds" was inspired by a 1978 Italian film that starred Bo Svenson ("Walking Tall, Part 2") and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson ("Black Caesar"). Tarantino's film, which he characterized to the Times as "not a remake," stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers. Cannes has been good to Tarantino; he won the Palme d'Or for "Pulp Fiction" 15 years ago. Buzz has been high on "Basterds" since Tarantino announced the project several years ago. "Taking Woodstock," the new film by "Brokeback Mountain" director Lee, is based on the book by Elliot Tiber, whose hotelier parents owned a musical festival permit in Bethel, New York, where Woodstock was held. The cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival was finally held. Other films in competition include Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," Jane Campion's "Bright Star" and Pedro Almodovar's "Broken Embraces."  Gallery: Some of Cannes' recent winners » . But this year's Cannes festival is attracting plenty of attention for its out-of-competition films as well. The festival is opening with "Up," the latest animated work from Pixar. "That sort of breaks convention to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon," Rozen said. Also at Cannes will be Heath Ledger's last film, "The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus." The Oscar-winning "Dark Knight" actor died during the making of the Terry Gilliam film; Gilliam managed to complete it by doing some rewriting and casting other actors -- including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp -- to play Ledger's part. Despite the interest in seeing Ledger, the film is still struggling to find a buyer, though Entertainment Weekly recently reported that a Los Angeles screening went over well. Cannes, which also functions as a huge film marketplace, may widen the net in attracting distributors. But much of the fun from Cannes comes from the films that emerge from nowhere. Recent winners of the Palme d'Or include 2000's "Dancer in the Dark," which established singer Bjork as an actress, and "4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days," a Romanian film that ended up topping many critics' lists in 2007. "One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments," Rozen said.

outputs.L1:
**(CNN) —** The economic downturn may take a toll on the 2009 Cannes Film Festival, which opens Wednesday night. But, as always, the show will go on.

Eli Roth and Brad Pitt are men on a mission in Quentin Tarantino’s *Inglourious Basterds*.

According to news reports, studios are scaling back parties and the accompanying glitz. Moreover, fewer people will be on hand to cover Cannes as news organizations worldwide cut costs. Several, in fact, have tightened their budgets by eliminating movie reviewers.

Nevertheless, attendees may be treated to a bumper crop of compelling and intriguing films, Variety’s Jay Weissberg told Reuters.

“We’ve all been hoping Cannes would pull something out of the bag to make us feel good again. On paper, they have.”

Leah Rozen, film critic for *People* magazine, said there are several promising contenders for the Palme d’Or, Cannes’ top prize, as well as a number of notable films premiering out of competition.

“What Cannes really is, is an international festival, and you really see world cinema,” she said. “This year, there are 52 films that are going to be represented, of which 20 are in competition.”

See Rozen discuss some of this year’s promising works ».

Two of the films in competition are American: Quentin Tarantino’s World War II movie, *Inglourious Basterds*, and Ang Lee’s *Taking Woodstock*, a story about the 1969 music festival.

Tarantino told *The New York Times* that he had long hoped to make a war movie.

“You’ve got to make a movie about something, and I’m a film guy, so I think in terms of genres,” he said.

However, the director of *Pulp Fiction* and *Jackie Brown* added that this does not mean the finished product resembles his original concept: “It’s simply the spark that starts the fire.”

*Inglourious Basterds* was inspired by a 1978 Italian film starring Bo Svenson (*Walking Tall, Part 2*) and football player-turned-actor Fred Williamson (*Black Caesar*). Tarantino’s film—which he described to the *Times* as “not a remake”—stars Brad Pitt and Mike Myers.

Cannes has been good to Tarantino: He won the Palme d’Or for *Pulp Fiction* 15 years ago. Anticipation for *Basterds* has been high since he announced the project several years ago.

*Taking Woodstock*, the new film from *Brokeback Mountain* director Lee, is based on the book by Elliot Tiber, whose hotelier parents owned a music-festival permit in Bethel, New York, where Woodstock was held. The cast includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch, Imelda Staunton and Eugene Levy as Max Yasgur, on whose farm the festival ultimately took place.

Other films in competition include Lars von Trier’s *Antichrist*, Jane Campion’s *Bright Star* and Pedro Almodóvar’s *Broken Embraces*.

Gallery: Some of Cannes’ recent winners ».

This year’s Cannes festival is also attracting considerable attention for its out-of-competition films. The festival will open with *Up*, the latest animated feature from Pixar.

“That sort of breaks convention, to open with what is, basically, a fancy cartoon,” Rozen said.

Also screening at Cannes will be Heath Ledger’s final film, *The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus*. The Oscar-winning *Dark Knight* actor died during production of the Terry Gilliam film. Gilliam managed to complete it through rewrites and by casting other actors—including Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp—to play Ledger’s part.

Despite interest in seeing Ledger, the film is still struggling to find a buyer, although *Entertainment Weekly* recently reported that a Los Angeles screening was well received. Cannes, which also serves as a major film marketplace, may broaden the film’s prospects for attracting distributors.

Much of Cannes’ appeal, however, comes from films that seemingly emerge from nowhere. Recent Palme d’Or winners include 2000’s *Dancer in the Dark*, which established singer Björk as an actress, and *4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days*, a Romanian film that ultimately topped many critics’ lists in 2007.

“One thing that always surprises me is that some of the films you have the lowest expectations for turn out to be terrific, and sometimes the bigger films turn out to be disappointments,” Rozen said.

News reports indicate that studios are reducing spending on lavish parties and related festivities. Fewer journalists are also expected to attend because media companies worldwide are trying to lower expenses; several organizations have even eliminated their film-critic positions.

Despite those cutbacks, attendees could be treated to an unusually strong and interesting selection of movies, Variety critic Jay Weissberg told Reuters. He said people had been hoping Cannes would deliver something uplifting and that, judging from the announced lineup, it appeared to have done so.

People magazine film critic Leah Rozen said several entries look like strong candidates for the Palme d’Or, the festival’s highest honor. She added that a number of noteworthy productions will also debut outside the official competition. Rozen emphasized that Cannes is truly global in scope and offers a broad view of filmmaking around the world. This year, 52 films will be presented, including 20 competing for the Palme d’Or. Rozen also discussed some of the year’s most promising titles.

Two American movies are among the competition entries: Tarantino’s World War II film “Inglourious Basterds” and Ang Lee’s “Taking Woodstock,” which tells a story connected to the 1969 music festival.

Tarantino told The New York Times that he had wanted to make a war film for many years. As someone who thinks about cinema through the lens of genre, he said, he needed a subject around which to build the movie. Still, the director of “Pulp Fiction” and “Jackie Brown” explained that the finished product does not necessarily resemble the idea with which he began; genre merely provides the initial inspiration.

“Inglourious Basterds” draws inspiration from a 1978 Italian movie featuring Bo Svenson, known for “Walking Tall, Part 2,” and former football player Fred Williamson, who became an actor and starred in “Black Caesar.” Tarantino told the Times that his version is not a remake. Its cast includes Brad Pitt and Mike Myers.

Cannes has previously rewarded Tarantino: 15 years earlier, “Pulp Fiction” received the Palme d’Or. Anticipation for “Basterds” has remained intense since he first announced the project several years ago.

“Taking Woodstock,” Lee’s follow-up as director of “Brokeback Mountain,” is adapted from Elliot Tiber’s book. Tiber’s parents operated a hotel and possessed a permit for a music festival in Bethel, New York, the community where Woodstock took place. The ensemble includes Liev Schreiber, Jeffrey Dean Morgan, Emile Hirsch and Imelda Staunton. Eugene Levy plays Max Yasgur, whose farm ultimately became the site of the festival.

The official competition also features Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist,” Jane Campion’s “Bright Star” and Pedro Almodóvar’s “Broken Embraces.” A gallery highlighted several recent Cannes winners.

Considerable attention is also being directed toward movies screening outside the competition. Cannes will begin with “Up,” Pixar’s newest animated feature. Rozen noted that choosing what is essentially an elaborate cartoon as the opening film departs from tradition.

Another Cannes selection is Heath Ledger’s final movie, “The Imaginarium of Dr. Parnassus.” Ledger, the Oscar-winning star of “The Dark Knight,” died before director Terry Gilliam had finished the production. Gilliam completed the film by revising the story and bringing in Jude Law, Colin Farrell and Johnny Depp to share aspects of Ledger’s role.

Although audiences are interested in seeing Ledger’s last performance, the film has continued to have difficulty securing a buyer. Entertainment Weekly, however, recently reported that a Los Angeles screening received a favorable response. Because Cannes also serves as a major international film market, its presence there could help the production reach a wider pool of potential distributors.

Part of Cannes’ appeal comes from unexpected discoveries—movies that arrive with little attention and suddenly stand out. Palme d’Or winners from recent years include the 2000 film “Dancer in the Dark,” which established singer Björk as an actress, and the Romanian drama “4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days,” which appeared at the top of many critics’ rankings in 2007.

Rozen said the festival repeatedly demonstrates how unpredictable expectations can be: films that initially seem least promising may prove excellent, while some of the most heavily promoted titles can end up disappointing.

# Cannes rolls out a leaner red carpet amid recession

**CANNES, France (CNN) —** Hollywood glamour, European auteurs and global cinema will converge on the French Riviera this week as the 62nd Cannes Film Festival opens under the shadow of the worldwide recession.

The May 13-24 event is expected to deliver its customary parade of stars, premieres and deal-making. But the economic downturn has forced studios, distributors and sponsors to rein in spending, with fewer extravagant parties, smaller promotional budgets and a more cautious mood at the festival’s film market.

Cannes will nevertheless begin on an upbeat note with Pixar’s **“Up,”** the first animated movie — and the first 3-D film — to open the festival.

The competition for the Palme d’Or features a formidable lineup of established filmmakers. Quentin Tarantino returns with the World War II drama **“Inglourious Basterds,”** starring Brad Pitt, while Ang Lee premieres the 1960s comedy-drama **“Taking Woodstock.”**

Other closely watched contenders include Lars von Trier’s controversial psychological horror film **“Antichrist,”** Pedro Almodóvar’s **“Broken Embraces,”** Michael Haneke’s **“The White Ribbon,”** Jane Campion’s John Keats drama **“Bright Star”** and Ken Loach’s **“Looking for Eric.”**

The competition also includes Park Chan-wook’s vampire thriller **“Thirst,”** Jacques Audiard’s prison drama **“A Prophet,”** Andrea Arnold’s **“Fish Tank”** and Marco Bellocchio’s historical drama **“Vincere.”** French actress Isabelle Huppert will lead the jury selecting the Palme d’Or winner.

Beyond the main competition, several high-profile premieres are expected to attract attention. Terry Gilliam will unveil **“The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus,”** featuring Heath Ledger’s final screen performance. Sam Raimi’s horror film **“Drag Me to Hell”** and Alejandro Amenábar’s historical epic **“Agora,”** starring Rachel Weisz, are also set for out-of-competition screenings.

The festival will close with **“Coco Chanel & Igor Stravinsky,”** Jan Kounen’s drama about the relationship between the French fashion designer and the Russian composer.

Even with fewer champagne-soaked celebrations and less corporate largesse, Cannes remains one of the film industry’s most important showcases. For filmmakers seeking financing and distributors hunting for the next international hit, the recession may make the stakes on the Croisette higher than ever.

## Cannes 2009: Tarantino, Pixar and Heath Ledger Take Center Stage

**CANNES, France —** The 62nd Cannes Film Festival delivered an unusually eclectic mix of Hollywood spectacle and auteur cinema, with Quentin Tarantino’s wartime fantasy **“Inglourious Basterds,”** Ang Lee’s counterculture comedy **“Taking Woodstock,”** Pixar’s animated adventure **“Up”** and Heath Ledger’s final film among the most closely watched premieres.

Tarantino returned to the festival with **“Inglourious Basterds,”** a revisionist World War II tale starring Brad Pitt as the leader of a Jewish-American commando unit hunting Nazis in occupied France. The film’s Cannes debut generated sharply divided reactions, but Christoph Waltz won widespread acclaim for his performance as the multilingual SS officer Hans Landa. Waltz ultimately received the festival’s **Best Actor** prize, launching an awards run that would later include an Academy Award.

**“Taking Woodstock,”** directed by Ang Lee, offered a lighter take on the era’s history. Based on Elliot Tiber’s memoir, the film follows a young man—played by Demetri Martin—whose family motel becomes entangled in the organization of the 1969 Woodstock festival. Rather than recreating the concert itself, Lee focused on the people and cultural upheaval surrounding it. The film competed for the Palme d’Or but drew mixed reviews.

Pixar made festival history with **“Up,”** the first animated film—and the first 3D feature—to open Cannes. Directed by Pete Docter, the movie follows elderly widower Carl Fredricksen, who uses thousands of balloons to fly his house toward South America, only to discover that a young Wilderness Explorer has joined him. Its emotional opening and inventive adventure won an enthusiastic reception, reinforcing Pixar’s reputation for combining family entertainment with adult themes.

The festival also hosted **“The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus,”** Heath Ledger’s final screen performance. Terry Gilliam’s fantasy was shown out of competition and carried particular emotional weight following Ledger’s death in January 2008. Because the actor had not completed filming, Johnny Depp, Jude Law and Colin Farrell stepped in to portray transformed versions of his character within the film’s magical world. The three actors donated their pay to Ledger’s daughter, Matilda.

Together, the premieres captured the range of Cannes 2009: a violent historical reinvention, a nostalgic look at the 1960s, a landmark animated opener and a poignant farewell to one of his generation’s most celebrated actors.

## Cannes 2009 preview: recession on the Croisette, auteurs on the screen

The 62nd Cannes Film Festival, running May 13–24, 2009, arrived at an awkward moment for an event synonymous with yachts, luxury hotels and lavish parties. The global financial crisis had not diminished the artistic ambitions of the festival’s official selection, but it was unmistakably changing the business and social machinery surrounding it.

Studios, distributors and television companies were cutting travel and entertainment budgets. Fewer junior executives and publicity staff were expected to make the trip, while companies that did attend were sending smaller delegations, renting less-expensive accommodation and reconsidering the costly beach parties, dinners and promotional stunts that traditionally competed with the films for attention. Trade advertising also contracted, and the Marché du Film faced buyers whose access to credit had tightened and whose appetite for risky independent acquisitions had weakened.

Cannes therefore promised to look busy without necessarily feeling as extravagant. Hotels and restaurants might still be full during the opening days, but the mood behind the glamour was likely to be cautious: fewer speculative purchases, more pressure on presales and a sharper focus on films with recognizable directors, stars or clearly marketable subjects.

Festival chief Thierry Frémaux acknowledged that the recession formed part of the background, but the official programme was designed to project continuity and confidence. Pixar’s **_Up_**, shown in 3-D, became the first animated feature—and the first 3-D film—to open Cannes. Its buoyant tone offered a deliberate contrast to the economic anxiety surrounding the festival.

### A competition crowded with major directors

Critics immediately noticed how heavily the competition relied on established Cannes names. Peter Bradshaw of *The Guardian* described the announced programme as a **“mouthwatering lineup,”** while trade coverage repeatedly characterized it as unusually auteur-heavy. Todd McCarthy of *Variety* viewed the gathering of internationally recognized filmmakers as evidence of Cannes’ enduring ability to attract what he called the **“heavy hitters”** of world cinema.

The list justified the enthusiasm. Quentin Tarantino returned with the Second World War fantasia **_Inglourious Basterds_**, starring Brad Pitt. Pedro Almodóvar brought the romantic noir **_Broken Embraces_**, with Penélope Cruz. Jane Campion presented the John Keats drama **_Bright Star_**; Michael Haneke unveiled the prewar German mystery **_The White Ribbon_**; Lars von Trier arrived with the psychological horror film **_Antichrist_**; and Ken Loach offered the football-inflected comedy-drama **_Looking for Eric_**.

They were joined by Jacques Audiard’s prison drama **_A Prophet_**, Ang Lee’s countercultural comedy **_Taking Woodstock_**, Alain Resnais’ **_Wild Grass_**, Marco Bellocchio’s Mussolini-era drama **_Vincere_**, Lou Ye’s **_Spring Fever_**, Park Chan-wook’s vampire film **_Thirst_**, Johnnie To’s thriller **_Vengeance_** and Gaspar Noé’s hallucinatory **_Enter the Void_**.

That concentration of famous directors was both a strength and a possible vulnerability. It gave recession-conscious distributors recognizable brands, but it also encouraged the complaint that Cannes was returning to a familiar circle rather than making room for enough discoveries. Several commentators described the selection as a kind of “greatest hits” programme of festival auteurs.

### International in reach, if uneven in representation

Despite its reliance on familiar names, Cannes remained more internationally expansive than almost any major film event. The official selection drew work from Europe, North America, Latin America, East Asia, the Middle East and Australia. French cinema was strongly represented, but the competition also included films from Spain, Britain, Germany, Austria, Italy, the United States, China, Hong Kong, South Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines, Israel and Palestine.

Critics saw that geographic spread as central to Cannes’ identity. Roger Ebert often called Cannes **“the greatest film festival in the world,”** emphasizing that its importance came not simply from glamour but from its function as a meeting point for national cinemas, critics, distributors and filmmakers. The 2009 programme supported that description: Hollywood stars shared the schedule with politically sensitive Chinese filmmaking, Asian genre cinema, European art films and work from territories that rarely received comparable global exposure.

The internationalism nevertheless had limits. Commentators noted the continued scarcity of women in the main competition. Jane Campion—the only woman ever to have won the Palme d’Or at that point—was the sole female director competing in 2009. The lineup was therefore broad geographically but much less diverse by gender.

### The films attracting the most anticipation

The loudest pre-festival excitement surrounded **_Inglourious Basterds_**. Tarantino had won the Palme d’Or for **_Pulp Fiction_** in 1994, and Cannes was a natural stage for his long-gestating war film. Its revisionist history, ensemble cast and Pitt-led star power guaranteed the festival’s most frenzied red carpet, even before anyone knew whether the film would be a masterpiece or an unruly indulgence.

Almodóvar’s **_Broken Embraces_** was another major attraction. The combination of Almodóvar and Cruz—coming soon after her Oscar win—gave Cannes both serious auteur credentials and international celebrity. Campion’s **_Bright Star_**, her account of the relationship between Keats and Fanny Brawne, was expected to provide a more restrained counterweight to Tarantino’s spectacle.

Haneke’s **_The White Ribbon_** generated intense curiosity because its story of mysterious violence in a German village before the First World War appeared to extend his longstanding interest in repression, guilt and social cruelty. Audiard’s **_A Prophet_** was less glamorous on paper but was widely tipped as a potential critical discovery because of the director’s reputation and the film’s forceful prison setting.

No film, however, seemed more likely to divide Cannes than von Trier’s **_Antichrist_**. Its combination of grief, sexuality, religious symbolism and graphic violence made it the festival’s most obvious provocation. Likewise, Noé’s **_Enter the Void_** promised an extreme sensory experience, while Park’s **_Thirst_** offered a more commercial collision of art cinema, eroticism and vampire horror.

Outside competition, Terry Gilliam’s **_The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus_** carried special emotional weight as Heath Ledger’s final film. Ledger died before completing his role, which was subsequently reworked with Johnny Depp, Jude Law and Colin Farrell appearing as transformations of the same character.

### A leaner Cannes, not a smaller cultural event

The recession was likely to reduce Cannes’ conspicuous consumption more than its cultural importance. There would be fewer extravagant corporate gestures, leaner publicity operations and a more conservative film market. Yet the festival itself had assembled a programme that few rivals could match: Tarantino, Almodóvar, Campion, Haneke, von Trier, Loach, Lee, Resnais, Audiard and Park in the same competition.

The central tension of Cannes 2009 was therefore clear. Economically, the festival was entering an era of austerity. Artistically, it was advertising abundance. The yachts might host fewer champagne receptions, but inside the Palais the expectation was that one of the decade’s most formidable Cannes lineups would keep the world’s attention fixed on the screen.
